The Lockman figure is a quoted outside statistic, left out.
facts: Eyal says the usual approach is a to-do list, and tasks tend to get pushed from one day to the next; he says to start from values instead and make time for them.
He sorts time into three life domains: you, relationships and work.

Timeboxing means deciding what you will do and when; the goal is a calendar with no white space, and success is measured by whether you did what you planned. 'You can't call something a distraction unless you know what it's distracting you from.'
Eyal and his wife Julie kept bickering about why household tasks weren't getting done; he admits he did less than his share and didn't see the tasks she handled.
Julie couldn't tell him how to help because working that out was itself work; evenings ended in late dinners, hurt feelings and sometimes tears.
On one of their date days they sat down and listed every household task each of them did, leaving nothing out; comparing her seemingly endless list with his was a wake-up call.
They agreed to split the jobs and timeboxed them on their schedules, leaving no doubt about when each would get done.
He also schedules time with his daughter: they wrote over a hundred activities on paper strips in a 'fun jar' and pull one every Friday afternoon; he and Julie schedule a date twice a month.
scene_details: two lists of household tasks side by side, one seemingly endless
a 'fun jar' of paper strips pulled every Friday afternoon
a calendar with no white space
tension: Eyal believed he valued equality at home, until he and his wife wrote their chores side by side.
opening_idea: Start at the table on a date day: two lists of household jobs, one much longer than the other.

lessons.idea: Give the things you value a time slot, not just a place on a list; a task with no time gets pushed to tomorrow.
lessons.anchor: The Eyals' chores only got done fairly once each one had a slot on the calendar.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: Two flatmates who argue about cleaning put 'bathroom, Saturday 10:00' in their shared calendar.

reflect_final: Which thing you say matters to you has no time on your calendar this week, and where could it go?

use_cases.situation: At home you keep arguing about who does what.
use_cases.move: Suggest each of you lists every task you do, as Eyal and his wife did, then put the split jobs on the calendar.

use_cases.situation: A colleague's to-do list keeps rolling over.
use_cases.move: Help them move the top two items into specific time blocks this week.
Block one slot for yourself and one for someone close before work fills the rest.

pocket_idea: A chore with a name and a time slot gets done; a chore on a list waits for whoever notices.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Nir Eyal thought he shared the housework fairly until he and his wife listed their chores side by side.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Nir Eyal and his wife kept arguing over chores, and evenings ended in late dinners and tears. On a date day they each listed every household task they did. Hers was seemingly endless. They split the jobs and put each one on the calendar with a time. In Indistractable he says that's the point: if it has no time, you can't even tell when you've been distracted from it.
